docTitle: HTTP status codes: read the first digit (Instagram)

slides.title: What the first digit of an HTTP status code *tells you*
slides.sub: A 4 means check the request. A 5 means check the server.

slides.title: Every response carries a three-digit *status code*
slides.body: The code tells you what happened, and the body gives you the detail. You can already tell a lot from the first digit.

slides.title: HTTP status codes at a bookshop counter
rows: We moved it to our other branch
Your request was fine, *our system broke*

slides.title: 2xx means it worked. Three you'll use all the time

calls.nm: Created, usually with a Location header
No Content, success with an empty body

slides.title: Which redirect? 301, 302, 307 or 308
slides.body: For normal web pages, 301 and 302 are fine. If you're redirecting an API where POST requests matter, I would use 307 and 308.

slides.title: 400 or 422?

cols.v: Broken JSON, like a missing bracket
The data inside makes no sense, like a book with no title

slides.body: Some APIs send 400 for validation errors too. I think 422 is clearer, because it tells the front end the format was fine and the data needs fixing.

slides.title: Ask for book 9999 when it doesn't exist, and you get a *404*
slides.body: 410 Gone says the book was there and it's gone for good.

slides.title: 401 asks who you are. 403 says *you can't do this*

cols.v: No hotel keycard at all, or the card doesn't work
Your card works fine, but it's for another room

slides.body: On a 401, send the user to log in. On a 403, logging in again with the same account won't help.

slides.title: Your app sends 500. The proxy sends 502 and 504

calls.nm: The proxy got an invalid answer from your app
Your app took too long, like a slow query

slides.title:
Never send
*200 OK* when something failed
slides.body: Your front end only sees the 200, and your monitoring counts it as a success. Send the real code and put the detail in the body.
